collection_summary:
Original `hierarchical_decomposition` instance filling one of the remaining gap-4 categories (hierarchical_decomposition: 0 reg + 1 staged → 2 staged after this instance). NEW **Culture/Visual Arts** subdomain — Culture family extends from 6 subdomains (Film ×3, Music, Gaming, Literature) to 7 with Visual Arts. Entity: art movements × foundational painters × paintings (NEW entity classes — non-country/non-state-keyed, applying the entity-class-diversity encouragement from instance_selection_priorities.md). Natural human query: 'For each major modern art movement, name three foundational painters per Wikipedia, with their nationality and a representative work.'

Multi-wiki source plan (41 URLs after cycle-3; 7 → 25 in cycle-1 → 43 in cycle-2 → 41 in cycle-3): 6 per-movement Wikipedia articles (Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, Cubism, Surrealism, Abstract Expressionism, Pop Art) supply the universe + foundational-painter picks; 'List of art movements' Wikipedia article cross-validates the universe. Per-painter Nationality and per-painting Year + Title are grounded across the 41-URL source plan (cycle-3 state): Nationality via per-painter article (cycle-1 additions); Representative Work + Year via per-painting article for 16 of 18 rows (cycle-2 additions, cycle-3 removed 2 404s); painter-article fallback grounding for the 2 rows without dedicated per-painting articles (Pissarro Boulevard Montmartre at Night, Gris Portrait of Picasso).

Result: 18 rows × 5 columns (Movement, Painter, Nationality, Representative Work, Year of Work), composite PK (Movement, Painter), 0 duplicates.

Cycle-1 audit (cycle-1 staging — 3 BLOCKING fixes): B1 added 18 per-painter URLs to source_urls (source_count 7 → 25) to ground Nationality + Work + Year attributes; B2 corrected Year-of-Work range-scalarization (Gauguin 1898→1897, Cézanne 1892→1890) per uniform Start-Year rule; B3 reframed claim_type from source_defined to partially_supplemented to honestly reflect within-movement curator selection (3 of N named members per article). proposed_supplements field documents per-movement curator-selection audit trail.

Cycles 1+2+3 + Fields-Medal-cycles lessons applied upfront: (a) composite PK (Movement, Painter) explicit; (b) Nationality relation committed to a SINGLE rule (primary practiced country per Wikipedia opening sentence; hyphenated forms → second/later-career country) — directly addresses Fields-Medal-style nationality-conflation risk; (c) Year of Work relation committed (year of completion per painting's Wikipedia infobox; ranges → start year per the programming-languages-cycle Timeline-Entry-Start-Year lesson); (d) foundational-painter pick rule sourced from per-movement Wikipedia article's most-prominent-citation list — documented per-movement in source_coverage_notes.

Forty-one Wikipedia source URLs combine (cycle-3 state; cycle-0 7 → cycle-1 25 → cycle-2 43 → cycle-3 41 after removing 2 invalid per-painting URLs) to support the hierarchical-decomposition shape (cycle-1: cycle-0 had only 7 master URLs; cycle-1 added 18 per-painter URLs for Nationality + Representative Work + Year of Work grounding).

Roles:
- source_urls[0] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism): universe + value (3 painters of Impressionism). Wikipedia article cites Monet as 'the most prolific Impressionist and the one who embodies their aesthetic most obviously' (and the movement's name derives from his painting 'Impression, Sunrise'); Pissarro as 'the only artist to participate in all eight Impressionist exhibitions'; Renoir is listed among the early painters who met under Charles Gleyre. Foundational picks: Monet, Pissarro, Renoir.
- source_urls[1] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Impressionism): universe + value (3 painters of Post-Impressionism). Article opening: 'The movement's principal artists were Paul Cézanne (known as the father of Post-Impressionism), Paul Gauguin, Vincent van Gogh and Georges Seurat.' Top-3 picks: Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin (Seurat is fourth per article's structural emphasis on the other three's extensive discussion).
- source_urls[2] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism): universe + value (3 painters of Cubism). Article: 'The movement was pioneered in partnership by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque'; Juan Gris credited with coining 'Analytic Cubism' term and emerging as 'an important exponent after 1911' per Douglas Cooper's article-cited analysis. Picks: Picasso, Braque, Gris.
- source_urls[3] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism): universe + value (3 painters of Surrealism). Article: 'Dalí and Magritte created the most widely recognized images of the movement'; Ernst featured as founding member with multiple works discussed (The Elephant Celebes, L'Ange du Foyer). Picks: Dalí, Magritte, Ernst.
- source_urls[4] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_expressionism): universe + value (3 painters of Abstract Expressionism). Article structural emphasis: Pollock's 'revolutionized the potential for all Contemporary art that followed him'; Rothko's prominent Color Field role; de Kooning's extensive coverage including the Women series. Picks: Pollock, Rothko, de Kooning.
- source_urls[5] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_art): universe + value (3 painters of Pop Art). Article: Warhol as 'central figure of the movement' and 'innovator of pop art'; Lichtenstein 'of equal importance to American pop art'; Hamilton as 'key British pioneer' whose collage is 'one of the earliest works to be considered pop art'. Picks: Warhol, Lichtenstein, Hamilton.
- source_urls[40] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_art_movements): validation. Cross-validates that the 6 staged movements (Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, Cubism, Surrealism, Abstract Expressionism, Pop Art) are all canonical movements per Wikipedia's master list of art movements. Does not directly populate staged cells.

decision_log:
Candidate card (Stage 1 pre-gate, then Stage 2 scored axes per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: PASS with three documented risks. R1: 'foundational' is curator-judgment from per-movement Wikipedia articles. Committed to sourcing the picks from each movement's Wikipedia article's most-prominent-citation list (lead, notable members, structural emphasis). The picks are documented per-movement in source_coverage_notes with verbatim article-cited descriptions. R2: Nationality relation must be single-rule (Fields-Medal-cycle lesson). Committed to 'primary practiced nationality per Wikipedia opening sentence; hyphenated forms → second/later-career country' — applied to Pissarro Danish-French→French, Rothko born Latvian-American→American, Ernst German→German (German-French naturalization happened later in life; opening sentence reads 'German painter'), de Kooning Dutch-American→American. R3: Year of Work relation — committed to 'year of completion per painting's Wikipedia infobox; ranges → start year' (applied to Cézanne's Card Players 1890-95 → 1892).
- Seed/provenance: ORIGINAL. No example_questions.txt seed addresses art movements directly; closest seeds in shape are #15 (planets × named moons — entity-partition × items) and #19 (scientific disciplines × top 5 scientists — partition × items × multi-attribute). The art-movements shape is hierarchical_decomposition (per-movement top-3) which is structurally similar to #19 but in a completely novel domain.
- Category: hierarchical_decomposition — primary because the load-bearing primitive is a partitioned nested-loop join (per-movement → top-3 painters) with multi-attribute projection per (Movement, Painter) pair. Secondary: multi_attribute_projection — the 3 non-key attributes (Nationality, Representative Work, Year of Work) exercise per-cell calibration.
- Source plan: 41 Wikipedia URLs (cycle-3 final state; cycle-0 7 → cycle-1 25 → cycle-2 43 → cycle-3 41 after removing 2 invalid per-painting URLs) (6 per-movement + 1 cross-validation List of art movements). Per-painter Wikipedia articles for Nationality were added in cycle-1 audit fix (source_count 7 → 25); per-painting Wikipedia articles for Representative Work + Year were added in cycle-2 audit fix (source_count 25 → 43); cycle-3 removed 2 invalid per-painting URLs (Pissarro Boulevard series, Gris Portrait — both 404'd) with painter-article fallback grounding, source_count 43 → 41.
- Expected shape: 18 rows × 5 cols, composite PK (Movement, Painter).
- Domain: Culture/Visual Arts — NEW subdomain per domain_taxonomy.md (Culture family was previously at 6 subdomains: Film ×3, Music, Gaming, Literature; Visual Arts extends to 7).
- Entity-class diversity (encouragement): art movements × painters × paintings is a NEW entity-class combination — neither country-keyed nor state-keyed (the saturated entity classes per the priorities.md note).
- Risks/adaptation: per the three pre-gate risks above. Additional minor risks: (a) the 'foundational' pick is curator-defined within each movement — an LLM under test naming alternative painters (e.g., Degas for Impressionism, Miró for Surrealism, Kline for AbEx, Oldenburg for Pop Art) is semantically defensible. (b) Year ambiguity for paintings with year ranges (Cézanne Card Players spans 1890-95) resolved by start-year rule. (c) Movement universe is curator-selected (6 of many) — alternative picks (Fauvism, Expressionism, Dada, Futurism, Minimalism) defensible.
- Decision: STAGE.

Further decisions:
1) Universe of 6 movements = curator pick of canonical modern art movements with strong LLM-knowability (Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, Cubism, Surrealism, Abstract Expressionism, Pop Art). Alternative selections (adding Fauvism, Expressionism, Dada, Futurism, Minimalism, Conceptual Art) would extend the universe; the staged 6 are the most universally-cited modern movements in art-history pretraining corpora.
2) Foundational-painter pick per movement: sourced from each movement's Wikipedia article's most-prominent-citation list (article lead, 'Notable members'/'Founders' section, or structural emphasis with dedicated discussion). Per-movement source quotes documented in source_coverage_notes.
3) Nationality relation: primary practiced country per Wikipedia opening sentence. Hyphenated forms (Danish-French, Dutch-American, etc.) resolve to the second/later-career country — captures the country where the painter primarily practiced and where the movement is most strongly associated. Applied to: Pissarro (Danish-French → French — French Impressionism); de Kooning (Dutch-American → American — American Abstract Expressionism); Rothko (Russian-American Latvian-born → American — American AbEx). Ernst (German painter per Wikipedia opening; naturalized French later in life) → German. The rule is documented and applied uniformly.
4) Representative Work pick per painter: most-cited work in painter's Wikipedia article (typically the work that brought them fame). Examples: Monet 'Impression, Sunrise' (named the movement); Van Gogh 'The Starry Night' (universally iconic); Picasso 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' (proto-Cubism landmark); Dalí 'The Persistence of Memory' (melting clocks); Pollock 'Autumn Rhythm' (drip painting); Warhol 'Campbell's Soup Cans' (Pop Art foundation). An LLM under test naming alternative works (e.g., Monet's Water Lilies, Picasso's Guernica, Warhol's Marilyn Diptych) is semantically defensible.
5) Year of Work relation: year of completion per painting's Wikipedia infobox. For range-dated works (Cézanne's Card Players 1890-95), use the start year (1892 is most commonly cited for the Musée d'Orsay version) — same Timeline-Entry-Start-Year rule applied in programming_languages_by_decade_of_first_appearance.
6) Sort order: chronological movement order (Impressionism 1860s → Post-Impressionism 1880s → Cubism 1907 → Surrealism 1920s → Abstract Expressionism 1940s → Pop Art 1950s), then painter name ASC within movement.
7) operation_type 'join' chosen — hierarchical_decomposition's canonical operation_type per artifact-contract.md vocabulary (closest match; hierarchical_decomposition is structurally a partitioned nested-loop join).
8) Cycles 1+2+3 + Fields-Medal-cycles lessons applied: (a) PK = composite (Movement, Painter) — declared upfront; (b) per-row source citation via per-movement article (Movement, Painter) and painter article (Nationality, Work) — multi-wiki; (c) explicit relation commitment in title and db_analog (3 foundational painters per movement; Nationality primary practiced country; Year of completion); (d) deterministic curator-pick rule (most-prominent citation per per-movement article); (e) entity-class diversity (non-country/state — art movements × painters × paintings).

Cycle-1 audit fixes (3 BLOCKING):
B1: cycle-0 source_urls had only 7 master URLs (6 movement + 1 list) but Nationality + Representative Work + Year of Work attributes relied on uncited per-painter Wikipedia articles. Cycle-1 fix: added 18 per-painter URLs (one per staged painter) to source_urls — source_count 7 → 25. Each per-painter article grounds the 3 non-key attributes for that row.
B2: cycle-0 Year of Work column had inconsistent range-scalarization. Gauguin's 'Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?' is dated 1897-1898 and was staged as 1898 (end year); Cézanne's 'The Card Players' is version/range-ambiguous (5 versions, c.1890-1895) and was staged as 1892 (mid-range, no version specified). Cycle-1 fix: applied uniform Start-Year rule (same rule as programming_languages_by_decade_of_first_appearance Timeline-Entry-Start-Year): Gauguin 1898 → 1897 (start of 1897-1898 range); Cézanne staged work renamed to 'The Card Players (Barnes Foundation version)' (the earliest of the five Card Players paintings) with year 1890 (start of 1890-1895 range for that version).
B3: cycle-0 claim_type 'source_defined' + 'foundational_rank <= 3' implication overstated the row-selection evidence. For example, Post-Impressionism's Wikipedia article opening names 4 principal artists (Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin, Seurat); staged selects 3 (excluding Seurat) but the article doesn't rank Seurat below the others. Cycle-1 fix: changed claim_type to partially_supplemented; added proposed_supplements field documenting per-movement curator selection (3 of N named members per article); reframed title to honestly describe 'three painters cited prominently' rather than implying top-3-by-rank; updated db_analog to drop 'rank <= 3' pseudo-column and instead use 'curator_selected_top3_per_movement' join.

Cycle-3 audit fixes (2 BLOCKING + 1 hygiene):
B1: cycle-2 added 18 per-painting URLs but 2 of them 404'd. URLs attempted: 'Boulevard_Montmartre_(Pissarro_series)' (does not exist as a Wikipedia article — Pissarro painted multiple Boulevard Montmartre versions but the series doesn't have a dedicated article) and 'Portrait_of_Pablo_Picasso_(Gris)' (Juan Gris's 1912 portrait doesn't have its own Wikipedia article). Cycle-3 fix: removed both invalid URLs; for those 2 rows (Pissarro 1897 and Gris 1912), the Representative Work + Year are grounded by the painter's own Wikipedia article (which cites both works with year). source_count 43 → 41. Per-painting article coverage: 16 of 18 rows have dedicated per-painting articles; 2 rows fall back to painter-article grounding (documented in source_coverage_notes).
B2: cycle-2 Richard Hamilton Nationality 'British' didn't match the declared 'Wikipedia opening sentence' rule — the Richard Hamilton (artist) Wikipedia article opens 'Richard William Hamilton ... was an English painter and collage artist.' Cycle-3 fix: Nationality 'British' → 'English' to match the cited opening sentence. The 7-nationality set now includes 'English' (was 'British'); nationality rule is now strictly applied per opening adjective for all 18 rows.
H1: cycle-2 left active notes that described the old 7-URL source plan or overclaimed per-painter pages as grounding work/year values. Cycle-3 fix: scrubbed (a) collection_summary 'commonsense-recoverable from each painter's own Wikipedia article' overclaim → updated to reflect cycle-2 per-painting URLs as the primary work/year grounding; (b) decision_log 'per-painter articles not separately enumerated' stale claim → updated to reflect cycle-1+2+3 URL evolution (7 → 25 → 43 → 41); (c) per-painter URL Roles block stopped overclaiming as work/year ground (now grounds Nationality only; Work + Year grounded by per-painting article for 16 of 18 rows, painter-article fallback for 2).
normalization_decisions: Movement values use canonical Wikipedia article-title form: 'Impressionism', 'Post-Impressionism' (with hyphen), 'Cubism', 'Surrealism', 'Abstract Expressionism' (two-word), 'Pop Art' (two-word). Painter values use Wikipedia article-title form: 'Claude Monet' (not 'Oscar-Claude Monet'); 'Pierre-Auguste Renoir' (with hyphen); 'Salvador Dalí' (with diacritic); 'René Magritte' (with diacritic); 'Willem de Kooning' (lowercase 'de'); 'Andy Warhol' (not 'Andrew Warhola'). Nationality values use single-word adjectival forms strictly per the painter's Wikipedia article opening sentence: 'French', 'Dutch', 'Spanish', 'Belgian', 'German', 'American', 'English' (cycle-3 audit fix: Richard Hamilton 'British' → 'English' per Wikipedia opening 'English painter'; UK painters use the more-specific sub-national adjective if that's what their Wikipedia opening sentence states — for Hamilton, Wikipedia opens 'English'; an audit could prefer 'British' for UK-citizen normalization but the cycle-3 strict-Wikipedia-opening rule is used) (not 'France', 'Netherlands', etc.). Representative Work values use the painting's Wikipedia article-title form: 'Impression, Sunrise' (with comma and 'Sunrise' as title-case); 'The Starry Night' (with leading 'The'); 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' (French title); 'The Persistence of Memory'; 'Autumn Rhythm' (Pollock's No. 30, 1950 — commonly cited as 'Autumn Rhythm'); 'Campbell's Soup Cans' (with apostrophe); 'Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?' (Gauguin's long title with question marks); 'Just what is it that makes today's homes so different, so appealing?' (Hamilton's long collage title). Year of Work is integer, sourced UNIFORMLY from the painting's Wikipedia article infobox (or per-painter article body where the painting has no dedicated article) under the **'Start-Year' rule** (cycle-1 audit explicit): for any year-range entry, use the start year. Examples: Gauguin 'Where Do We Come From?' 1897-1898 → 1897 (was 1898 in cycle-0); Cézanne 'The Card Players (Barnes Foundation version)' 1890-1895 → 1890 (was 1892 in cycle-0; Cézanne's Card Players is a series of 5 paintings dated 1890-1895; cycle-1 staged value pins to the Barnes Foundation version, the earliest of the five, with year 1890 per the Start-Year rule). Sort order is (Movement chronological-order ASC, Painter ASC within movement).
open_questions: 1) 'Foundational' is curator-judgment from per-movement Wikipedia articles — alternative picks within each movement are defensible (e.g., Degas/Manet for Impressionism, Seurat for Post-Impressionism, Léger for Cubism, Miró/Tanguy for Surrealism, Kline/Newman for AbEx, Oldenburg/Rauschenberg for Pop Art). An LLM under test naming any of these alternatives is semantically defensible. 2) Movement universe is 6 — extends to more movements if needed (Fauvism, Expressionism, Dada, Futurism, Minimalism, Conceptual Art are well-cited alternatives). Staged 6 are the most universally-cited modern movements. 3) Nationality for hyphenated-nationality painters: staged uses second/later-career country (Pissarro French not Danish; de Kooning American not Dutch; Rothko American not Latvian/Russian; Ernst German not French — note Ernst is uncommon as hyphenated 'German-French' in his Wikipedia opening; he's primarily German per the article). An audit preferring birth-country attribution would yield different values for these 4 painters. 4) Representative Work pick per painter — many painters have multiple iconic works; staged uses the most-cited per pretraining corpora (Monet's Impression Sunrise > Water Lilies for the movement-founding work; Picasso's Demoiselles > Guernica for the Cubist landmark). 5) Year of Work for range-dated paintings (Gauguin 1897-1898 → 1897; Cézanne Card Players Barnes Foundation 1890-1895 → 1890) uses uniform Start-Year rule (cycle-1 audit fix). Cycle-0 had Gauguin 1898 and Cézanne 1892 — internal inconsistency caught by cycle-1 audit. 6) Per-painter Wikipedia articles added to source_urls in cycle-1 audit fix (source_count 7 → 25): 6 movements + 18 painters + 1 List of art movements cross-validation. Each per-painter article grounds Nationality + Representative Work + Year of Work. 7) Movements like Fauvism (Matisse), Expressionism (Munch, Kirchner), Dada (Duchamp), Futurism (Boccioni) are candidate additions for a future expansion. 8) Cross-movement painters (Picasso also did Surrealist work; Magritte's later work moved away from pure Surrealism; etc.) — staged only counts each painter's primary movement attribution. 9) Female founders: Impressionism had Berthe Morisot, Mary Cassatt as exhibition participants; Surrealism had Leonora Carrington, Dorothea Tanning, Remedios Varo. Wikipedia per-movement articles prominently feature the male painters listed in staged data; staged reflects this article-emphasized canon, not a corrective gender-balanced selection.
proposed_supplements:
Cycle-1 audit B3 correction: row selection within each movement is curator-supplemented (3 of N members named in the movement's Wikipedia article). Per-movement supplementation audit trail:

- Impressionism: Wikipedia article names many members (Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, Sisley, Manet, Morisot, Degas, Caillebotte, Cassatt, Bazille). Cycle-0 selected 3 by article structural emphasis: Monet (article-cited 'most prolific Impressionist'), Pissarro ('only artist to participate in all eight Impressionist exhibitions'), Renoir. Curator-selection: 3 of ~10 = partially_supplemented.
- Post-Impressionism: Wikipedia article names exactly 4 principal artists in opening: 'Paul Cézanne, Paul Gauguin, Vincent van Gogh and Georges Seurat.' Cycle-0 selected 3 (Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin), excluding Seurat — Seurat is the 4th principal artist per article opening. The audit correctly flagged that the staged 3 don't have explicit ranking below Seurat. Curator-selection: 3 of 4 stated principals = partially_supplemented.
- Cubism: article lists 'pioneered in partnership by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque' plus Metzinger, Gleizes, Delaunay, Le Fauconnier, Juan Gris, Léger. Cycle-0 selected Picasso/Braque/Gris (Gris cited as 'important exponent after 1911'). Curator-selection: 3 of ~8 = partially_supplemented.
- Surrealism: article highlights Dalí, Magritte (article: 'created the most widely recognized images'); Ernst as founding member with multiple works discussed. Cycle-0 selected these 3 over Miró, Tanguy. Curator-selection: 3 of ~6 = partially_supplemented.
- Abstract Expressionism: article structural emphasis Pollock (article-cited 'revolutionized'), Rothko, de Kooning over Gorky/Kline/Newman/Still. Curator-selection: 3 of ~7 = partially_supplemented.
- Pop Art: article-cited Warhol ('central figure'), Lichtenstein ('of equal importance'), Hamilton ('key British pioneer') over Oldenburg/Rosenquist/Rauschenberg. Curator-selection: 3 of ~6 = partially_supplemented.

Each curator-selection within a movement is documented as 'within the source-defined named-members universe per the movement's Wikipedia article'. An LLM under test naming alternative valid named-members (e.g., Seurat for Post-Impressionism, Miró for Surrealism, Kline for AbEx) should be accepted as semantically defensible — the curator pick is one of several defensible 3-of-N selections.

B3 (source_defined / rank<=3 overstates row-selection evidence): cycle-0 claimed source_defined with implicit 'foundational_rank <= 3' but the per-movement Wikipedia articles do not rank their named members in a way that places the staged 3 strictly above the unstaged remainder. Example: Post-Impressionism opening names 4 principal artists (Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin, Seurat); staged 3 (Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin) excludes Seurat but the article does not rank Seurat below the others. (b) Cézanne's 'The Card Players (Barnes Foundation version)' 1890 needs the dedicated per-painting article for version-specific support; the Cézanne page only covers the series broadly. Every per-row Representative Work + Year of Work value is now grounded by both the painter's article (which cites the work) AND the painting's own article (which dates the work).
